---
title: "GPU execution"
subtitle: "Experimental device dispatch through ExecContext"
execute:
  enabled: false
---

A handful of Marrow's kernels can run on the GPU — Metal on Apple Silicon, CUDA
on NVIDIA — through Mojo's `DeviceContext`. This is **experimental**: the GPU
and CPU paths share the same kernel source, and only a few kernels are wired up
so far. Treat it as infrastructure to build on, not a turnkey speed-up.

::: {.callout-note}
The code on this page is Mojo. GPU dispatch is a native-level capability driven
by an `ExecContext`; it is not exposed as a distinct mode in the Python
bindings today.
:::

## What can run on the GPU

Device dispatch is implemented for element-wise kernels only:

| Kernel group | GPU path | Notes |
|--------------|:--------:|-------|
| Arithmetic (`add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, …) | yes | via `elementwise[target="gpu"]` |
| Comparisons (`equal`, `less`, `greater`, …) | yes | returns a `BoolArray` |
| Hashing | yes | used by the hash-table kernels |
| Sort, join, aggregate, filter | no | CPU only |

## ExecContext

Every kernel that can use a device takes an `ExecContext` as its last
argument. It bundles two independent choices — CPU worker count and an optional
GPU device — behind three factory methods:

```mojo
from marrow.execution import ExecContext
from gpu.host import DeviceContext

var cpu       = ExecContext.serial()            # single-threaded CPU
var threaded  = ExecContext.parallel(num_threads=0)  # 0 = all cores
var on_device = ExecContext.gpu(DeviceContext())     # run on the GPU
```

The default constructor (`ExecContext()`) is serial CPU with no device.

```mojo
from marrow.kernels.arithmetic import add
from marrow.arrays import array
from marrow.dtypes import int64

var a = array[int64]([1, 2, 3, 4])
var b = array[int64]([10, 20, 30, 40])

var cpu_result = add(a, b, ExecContext.serial())
var gpu_result = add(a, b, ExecContext.gpu(DeviceContext()))
```

## Device transfer

Transfers are explicit, so you always know when data crosses the bus:

| Method | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `PrimitiveArray[T].to_device(ctx)` | upload array data to the GPU |
| `PrimitiveArray[T].to_host(ctx)` | download it back to the CPU |
| `Buffer.to_device(ctx)` / `Bitmap.to_device(ctx)` | low-level transfers |

A kernel result produced on the device is device-resident (null host pointer,
device buffer set); call `.to_host(ctx)` before reading it on the CPU.

## When it is (and isn't) worth it

The kernels wired to the GPU today are all **low arithmetic intensity** — roughly
one operation per element. For those, moving data to and from the device usually
costs more than it saves, and CPU SIMD is competitive or faster. The GPU path
becomes interesting only when the data is *already* resident on the device and
several kernels run over it before the result is read back.

## Caveats

- **Null bitmaps are not propagated on the device.** GPU binary kernels compute
  values only; null-aware arithmetic is CPU-only for now. Use the CPU path when
  either input has nulls.
- Coverage is narrow — sorting, joins, aggregation and filtering have no GPU
  path.
